job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Adam Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six. I open the family shop with my father, which sells stationery and does printing, on Mill Street in Marlow, and I stand at the till until eleven. Then I go home, put on a clean shirt and do job applications at the dining table. On Sundays we go to church and have lunch at my grandmother's. I live with my parents and my younger sister Yui.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Accounting, a good result. I spent six weeks at a small firm called Pryce and Sons, doing bookkeeping for local shops, mostly by hand and in the firm's old software. I enjoyed it, and Mr Pryce told me I had a careful eye. I don't use AI tools. I don't see why I'd need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought. In the shop I'd tell my father the noise was people selling something. To my friends I'd say work hard, keep your head down and the world keeps needing honest accountants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel a bit of relief but not much. Real life is still the same: no offer after months, parents who keep saying not to worry, and me watching the postman. A little routine work gets automated, but I don't think it touches careful people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd apply to ten firms a week, call Mr Pryce every month, and visit the small firms on our street and hand my CV over in person. I'd keep working the till three mornings a week so I'm useful. And I'd go to the evening class for the professional exam, because it's respectable and it gives me a goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit ashamed. My father didn't have to look for work, and I'm still doing it at 23.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hand your CV over in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you hand your CV over in person?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the shame feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a name on a screen can be deleted, and a person at the desk can't. I think a firm trusts someone who turns up. My father always says people buy from people they've seen, and I think hiring works the same way.

say: I'd say that's what I thought: the noise was **people selling something**.
I'd tell friends to work hard and keep their heads down.
think: I feel a little relief, but the real problem is **no offer** after months.
Routine work gets automated, though I doubt it touches careful people.
do: Apply to **ten firms** a week and call Mr Pryce every month.
Hand my CV in **person** at small firms on our street.
Work the shop till three mornings a week and take the evening exam class.
feel: **Steady** but a bit ashamed that I'm still looking at 23.

steps.text: Hand my CV in person to small firms on Mill Street
Call Mr Pryce at the accountancy firm every month
Attend the evening class for the professional exam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've seen change before and good people got through it. I'd tell my father the shop should keep its human side, like knowing customers by name. At church I'd say look after each other, because some of us will lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. The bookkeeping I did at Pryce and Sons is exactly what software handles well. If the firm's clients get it done by a program, the firm needs fewer people, and I'm at the bottom of the list. I don't like it, and I don't like that I'm slow to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to firms that serve people and not computers, like small family businesses and farm accountants. I'd ask Mr Pryce to show me the software his firm uses, face to face, since I can't pick it up from a screen. And I'd offer to do the shop's accounts for a small wage, so I have something to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. It feels like a storm I can see on the horizon, and I'm standing in a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How slow would you be with the software, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How slow would you be with the software, really?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your sister Yui do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slower than my sister, definitely. I read the whole manual first, then try one thing, then ask someone. A younger person just clicks around. But once I understand something I don't forget it, and I make fewer mistakes.

say: I'd say we've seen change before and good people got through it.
I'd tell my father to keep the shop's **human side**, and tell church friends to look after each other.

Ask Mr Pryce to show me his firm's software **face to face**.
Offer to do the shop's accounts for a small wage.
feel: **Unsettled**, like seeing a storm on the horizon while standing in a field.

fieldNote: Knows his own pace: **slow to start**, accurate afterwards.

steps.text: Apply to farm accountants and small family firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong that something this big comes without a plan. I'd tell people at church to pray, but also to check the savings and help one another. And I'd write to the council about retraining for people whose jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm alarmed. Within two years my degree might be nothing, and I haven't learned the tools. My father's shop will survive a while, as people still want printing and pens, but it's small and it won't pay for three adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every bit of my savings in the bank, and take a job at the till full time while I looked for something else. I'd apply for anything where I'd be in the room with customers, like a bank counter or a pension office. And I'd marry sooner than I planned, if my girlfriend Aiko said yes, because I'd want us to face it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I wouldn't tell my parents, because I'd not want them to carry it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tell Aiko but not your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you tell your girlfriend and not your parents?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the shop full time that would be useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Aiko and I plan to build a life together, so she has a right to know where I stand. My parents will worry for me for ever, and I don't want them lying awake over something I can't fix.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** for something this big to come without a plan.
I'd urge people at church to pray, check savings and write to the council about retraining.
think: Within two years my degree might be **nothing**, and I haven't learned the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and sensible people use fair warning. I'd tell my friends to learn something that keeps its value, like a trade or a profession people trust. At church I'd say we should start a small fund to help families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still anxious but it's an anxiety I can plan around. If I find a job within the year, I can get my professional qualification, and I'd have people around me who'd teach me the tools. After five years I might be someone the firm needs, not just someone it tolerates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any honest accounting job, even a poorly paid one, and work my way up. I'd do my exams in the evening, learn the software from a colleague I trust, and save a third of my pay. I'd also keep my hours at the shop so my father isn't left alone. And I'd put money towards a deposit with Aiko.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A weight on the chest, but I can carry it. At least I'd know the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew the exact date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew the exact date?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep your father from being left alone in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan backwards from it. Two years to the qualification, a year in a firm, a deposit saved by year four. A date is something a careful person can work with. It's the surprise that I can't stand.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** and sensible people use it.
I'd urge friends to learn something that keeps its value and start a small fund at church.

fieldNote: Hates **surprise** more than risk, which explains his resistance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a generation's worth of time to prepare, and we shouldn't waste it. I'd tell young people to learn a skill, marry well, and build something that's theirs. I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly settled. I could finish my qualification, work a few years at a good firm, and one day take over my father's shop or start a small practice. The danger is the last four years, when the thinking tools are everywhere, and I'd want to be prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job within the year, pass the exams by 26, and keep my hours at the shop. I'd marry Aiko in about three years, and I'd buy a small place near my parents. I'd learn the software properly at work, one tool at a time. And I'd keep saving, because a cushion matters in any scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, almost. It's the closest to the life I'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really want to take over your father's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you really want to take over the shop?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good marriage with Aiko look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like the choice. A shop that prints weddings and school forms will last as long as people want paper, which is still quite a while. I'd run my father's shop as the accountant, and he could stay on the front counter for as long as he liked.

I'd back apprenticeships, not handouts, and tell young people to build something their own.
think: I'd feel fairly settled: qualification, a good firm, then my father's shop or a small **practice**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because I'm slow to learn and it leaves no time to catch up. What would help is a real route for beginners, such as apprenticeships in firms, and some warning from employers about what they plan to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I seem stubborn, and I know it. I'm not against new things. I'm against being told I'm behind by people who didn't wait for me.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things. I'm against being told I'm behind by people who didn't wait for me.
portrait: Adam is 23, an accounting graduate who works the till at his parents' shop in Marlow, with no offer yet.
He avoids AI tools and trusts handshakes, in-person CV drops and careful, **slow learning**.
His traditional views favour family, faith, apprenticeships and savings over handouts.
In the fast scenario he is alarmed and hides his fear from his parents, sharing only with his girlfriend **Aiko**.
With ten years he feels peaceful and imagines running the shop as its **accountant**.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because he is slow to learn and has no time to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: Warning from employers about what they plan to do.
